title: Formed Drexel, Morgan & Co. with Anthony Joseph Drexel
statement: At Junius Morgan's urging, took Anthony J. Drexel as his mentor and senior partner, forming Drexel, Morgan & Co. in New York to act as agent for European capital flowing into American railroads and industry.
outcome: The partnership created a national capital market for industrial companies, underwrote the U.S. Army's pay in 1877, and after Drexel's death was renamed J.P. Morgan & Co. in 1895, today JPMorgan Chase.

title: Orchestrated the Edison-Thomson Houston merger that created General Electric
statement: Having financed the 1889 consolidation of Edison's electrical companies into Edison General Electric, merged that company with Charles Coffin's Thomson-Houston Electric Company to form General Electric.
outcome: GE became one of the original twelve companies on the Dow Jones Industrial Average in 1896 and remained in the index for 122 years, one of the twentieth century's most influential industrial corporations.

title: Formed the United States Steel Corporation by buying Carnegie Steel
statement: Merged Carnegie Steel, Federal Steel, and National Steel in a 492-million-dollar transaction, installing Charles M. Schwab as president and Elbert H. Gary as chairman.
outcome: U.S. Steel became the world's first billion-dollar corporation, capitalized at 1.4 billion dollars, producing roughly two-thirds of American steel in its founding year.

title: Financed the International Mercantile Marine shipping trust
statement: Bankrolled the formation of the International Mercantile Marine Company, absorbing the American, Red Star, Atlantic Transport, Leyland, and White Star lines in an attempt to dominate transatlantic shipping.
outcome: The monopoly design failed against the nature of sea transport, antitrust law, and the British agreement; overleveraged, the trust entered receivership in 1915 after the Titanic disaster, its remnants becoming the United States Lines.

title: Organized the Wall Street rescue that ended the Panic of 1907
statement: Returning from a Richmond church convention, convened the city's bank and trust presidents in his library, forced a plan of pooled loans, and directed cash to the stock exchange's loan post; later locked bankers overnight until the trusts funded their weakest members.
outcome: The panic was over by November 7, 1907, though Morgan himself lost 21 million dollars; the rescue's dependence on one man spurred the Aldrich-Vreeland Act and ultimately the Federal Reserve Act of 1913.

title: Testified before the Pujo Committee on the money trust
statement: Though in ill health, appeared before the House subcommittee in December 1912 and faced days of questioning by counsel Samuel Untermyer, defending a banking industry built on character and trust rather than money or property.
outcome: The committee found 180 individuals holding 341 directorships across 112 corporations with 22.245 billion dollars in resources; associates blamed the hearings' stress for Morgan's decline, and he died on March 31, 1913.

title: Commissioned Charles McKim to build the Morgan Library
statement: Rejected baroque and temple designs and told McKim he wanted a gem, insisting on marble construction, Tennessee marble over white, and dry masonry at an extra fifty thousand dollars, while forbidding workers to speak to the press.
outcome: The 1.2-million-dollar library opened in 1906, hosted the overnight 1907 rescue sessions, and was incorporated by Jack Morgan as a public institution in 1924; today's Morgan Library & Museum holds more than 350,000 objects.

title: Passed the House of Morgan to J. P. Morgan Jr.
statement: Died in Rome on March 31, 1913, leaving the banking business and the fortune, including about thirty million dollars in bank shares, to his son Jack, who had managed the London end of the firm.
outcome: Jack led the firm through the First World War financing of the Allies, but the Glass-Steagall Act of 1933 later split the House of Morgan into J.P. Morgan & Co., Morgan Stanley, and Morgan Grenfell.
